newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma puts banker in charge of reforms.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma puts banker in charge of reforms.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma on Tuesday put a leading young banker with roots in industry in charge of economic reforms in the former Soviet republic.
Sergei Tigipko, head of Privatbank, one of Ukraine's top five banks, will take over from Viktor Pynzenyk.
Kuchma's press spokesman Dmitro Markov said Tigipko, 37, had been appointed deputy prime minister in a presidential decree.
The text of the decree did not outline Tigipko's duties but it followed Pynzenyk's resignation from the post of deputy prime minister in charge of economic reform.
The resignation of Pynzenyk, who quit in anger last week at slow progress in getting the budget and a tax reform package passed, caused dismay among Western analysts.
Tigipko, 37, is a metallurgist by education from the central industrial city of Dnipropetrovsk, where his bank is situated and Kuchma once ran the Soviet Union's largest missile plant.

The appointment appeared designed to ease relations between Kuchma, who says he is completely for reforms, and a parliament dominated by conservatives where Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko has broad support.
Lazarenko, blamed by Kuchma for the absence of this year's budget, also started his political career in Dnipropetrovsk and local media have linked him to Privatbank.

Tigipko, who has worked in the sector since 1990, made Privatbank one of Ukraine's most profitable last year and pushed its starting capital to 30 million hryvnias ($16.5 million) at the end of 1996 from 10 million hryvnias a year earlier.
One analyst said late on Tuesday Pynzenyk's departure was "a disaster for Ukraine" but gave a cautious welcome to Tigipko's appointment.
"Pynzenyk's name stood for reforms in the West and Tigipko has yet to achieve such recognition. But it's not the worst solution," he said.
Pynzenyk, 44, is an economics professor who was so devoted to pulling Ukraine out of decline he kept a bed in his office because of the long hours he spent there.

When Kuchma accepted his resignation on Monday on Pynzenyk's insistence, Pynzenyk said the economy was at a turning point and accused parliament and government of lacking the will to get approved the budget and tax reforms he created.
Without this year's budget and the tax reforms, Ukraine cannot win approval for a $2.5-$3 billion Extended Fund Facility loan from the International Monetary Fund.
Kuchma at the weekend warned that the economy would collapse without foreign credits.
The tax reforms were first presented to parliament last November but parliament sent them back to the government and says it is still waiting for a new version to approve.
